messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Kofi

Kofi was fifty-two when he walked into the office, though his bearing made him seem older. He had been a plumber for twenty-eight years—the kind of man who knew the bones of buildings, who could diagnose a problem by sound alone, who took pride in the steadiness of his hands and the reliability of his reputation. That identity had anchored him through a long marriage to Ama, through raising two children in a modest neighborhood outside Atlanta, through the small satisfactions of a trade well-practiced. Three years ago, that identity began to collapse.

The assault happened on a Thursday evening in October. Kofi had been called to a residential job in a part of town he did not know well—a basement pipe replacement that would take two hours, maybe three. He was alone, as he usually was. The homeowner had left him the keys and said he would be back by nine. Around seven-thirty, as Kofi was finishing up, a man came down the basement stairs with a knife. Kofi never saw his face clearly. What he remembers, what returns to him in fragments of image that he cannot quite string into sentences, is the blade catching the fluorescent light, the man's arm moving, the shock of pain across his ribs, the sound of his own voice—a sound he did not recognize—crying out. He was stabbed four times. A neighbor heard him calling for help and the man fled. Kofi spent two weeks in the hospital and another six weeks recovering at home.

The police investigation went nowhere. No arrest was made. The case file grew cold. Kofi came to believe that what had happened to him did not matter, that the world had decided his suffering was not worth the effort to address. This belief took root and spread like an infection through everything he thought about himself and his circumstances.

Within weeks of returning to work, Kofi found he could no longer move freely through his day. He began taking jobs only in areas he knew, in neighborhoods where he had worked before, where he could control the variables. His clients started to notice he was declining jobs, becoming selective in ways he never had been. His supervisor asked if everything was alright. Kofi said yes, but what he meant was that he could not manage the feeling of exposure, the sense that danger lived in unfamiliar spaces, that his body was no longer his to trust in the world. He came to feel safe only at home, in his basement workshop, and in the few commercial buildings where he had worked for years. Anywhere else, his chest would tighten.

The startle responses came without warning. A coworker moving quickly past him on a job site sent him into a state of acute fear that lasted hours. The sound of someone running up stairs behind him made his vision narrow. He became hypervigilant to movement in his peripheral vision, interpreting every sudden gesture as a threat. Ama learned not to touch him from behind. His children, when they visited, stayed quiet.

Sleep became a battlefield. Kofi would lie awake until two or three in the morning, his mind cycling through images he could not articulate—the blade, the stairwell, the man's silhouette—and a crushing sense of shame that he could not explain. He had been helpless. He had been hurt in his own body, in a space where he was working, doing the thing that defined him, and no one had been held accountable. When he finally slept, the images followed him. He woke in a cold sweat, often with the conviction that something terrible was about to happen.

What frightened him most was not the memory itself but what the memory suggested about him: that he was no longer the man he had been, that he could not trust his own judgment anymore, that he had somehow failed in a way he could not articulate or forgive. He had been strong. He had been capable. Now, at fifty-two, he felt like a man diminished, confined to a shrinking world, unable to do the work that had always meant something to him. His income had dropped by nearly forty percent. Ama had stopped asking when he would feel better.

It was Ama who finally insisted he come in. She said he was disappearing, that the man she married was becoming a ghost in his own house. Kofi came because he had run out of other options, because the guilt and the rage and the trapped feeling had begun to feel like they might consume him entirely.
